title: Generations
summary: The five consumer generations, their size, wealth, media habits and what they expect from brands. Interviewers use generational shorthand constantly; this lets you use it precisely and avoid lazy stereotypes.

blocks.title: The generations at a glance
rows: Retiring; hold the most wealth; heavy healthcare, travel, grandparent spending
Peak earning; teens/college kids at home, aging parents
Family formation, first homes, young kids
Students and early career; fastest-growing spending power
Kids; influence parents' spending via YouTube, gaming
blocks.note: Boomer/Gen X/Millennial ranges per Pew and the Federal Reserve. Pew starts Gen Z in 1997; 2012 is the common end year. Gen Alpha is not formally defined by Pew. Population estimates are Census-based, via Visual Capitalist.

blocks.title: Spending power vs wealth
blocks.body: Population size and wealth are not the same. Boomers held ~51% of US household wealth in 2025, while Millennials and Gen Z together held only ~10% despite being the largest cohorts (Fed Distributional Financial Accounts). Younger households out-earn their parents at the same age, but older households own the homes and stock portfolios. A multi-decade 'great wealth transfer' to heirs is a recurring theme in wealth-management and luxury cases.

blocks.title: Channel and media habits
items: YouTube (~84% of adults) and Facebook (~71%) are the only platforms used by a majority of every age group (Pew, 2025).
About 8 in 10 adults aged 18-29 use Instagram vs ~19% of those 65+.
Roughly half of 18-29 year-olds visit TikTok daily, vs ~5% of adults 65+ (Pew, 2025).
Facebook usage peaks among 30-49 year-olds (~80%), making it a Millennial and Gen X channel.
Boomers still over-index on linear TV, email and physical stores; Gen Z discovers products via creators and search on social.

blocks.title: Brand expectations by generation
rows: Quality, service, trust, clear value; phone and in-store help
Practicality, reliability, time savings for busy households
Convenience, reviews, loyalty programs, family-friendly value
Price fatigue on subscriptions and delivery fees
Authenticity, creators, community, wellness, value for money
Low loyalty; quick to churn and to call out brands

blocks.title: Behaviors worth knowing
items: Gen Z and Millennials are ~36% of US adults but ~41% of wellness spending (McKinsey, 2025).
Over half of Gen Z and Millennials canceled a streaming service within six months (Deloitte, 2025); churn-and-return is normal.
Adults 18-34 report drinking alcohol at ~50%, and two-thirds view moderate drinking as unhealthy (Gallup, 2025).
Gen Z is the most racially and ethnically diverse adult generation so far (Pew).

blocks.title: Generations are a proxy, not a cause
blocks.body: Much 'generational' behavior is really life stage (students rent, parents buy minivans) or income. In a case, say 'younger consumers at this life stage' and check whether the effect holds as they age. Avoid sweeping claims like 'Gen Z doesn't care about price'; surveys show they are very price-aware.

blocks.title: Use cohort size plus wallet
blocks.body: When asked which generation to target, compare cohort size, spend per person in the category, and growth. Boomers win on wealth today, Millennials on household formation, Gen Z on future value and influence. Saying this trade-off explicitly signals structured thinking.

in_a_case: A legacy apparel brand losing share: check whether its core buyers are aging Boomers/Gen X while Gen Z discovers rivals on TikTok and Instagram.
Wealth management growth: the transfer of Boomer wealth to Gen X and Millennial heirs is a retention risk and opportunity.
Beverage or alcohol strategy: lower drinking among young adults pushes non-alcoholic and functional drinks.
Streaming or subscription cases: young households churn more, so model lifetime value with churn-and-return, not a fixed lifespan.
Kids' products: Gen Alpha influences purchases but parents pay; marketing must work for both and respect children's privacy rules.
